their_construct: RubricBench: 1,147 人工筛选的困难 pairwise 偏好样本，每个样本配一份专家标注、仅由 instruction 推导、原子化二元(Yes/No)的 gold rubric（每条样本平均约 3-6 个 rubric item，见 Fig.2）。三种受控条件对比：Vanilla / Self-Generated Rubric / Human-Annotated Rubric，backbone、prompt、decoding 全固定。覆盖被直接操作化为 Rubric Recall：被生成 rubric 至少匹配到一条的 gold item 数 / gold item 总数（Appendix B.1）。并定义 Hallucination Rate（生成项匹配不到任何 gold 项的比例）与 Structural F1。模型：4 类 RM（ArmoRM/InternLM2/Tulu-3、Nemotron、RM-R1）、LLM-as-judge（GPT-4o-mini、DeepSeek-v3.2、Gemini-3-Flash 等）、rubric-aware 流水线（Auto-Rubric、RocketEval、CheckEval、TICK、OpenRubric）。
their_finding: 主结论是下游 pairwise 判别精度上的『Rubric Gap』：同一 backbone 只换 rubric 来源，human-annotated rubric 相对最优自动方案稳定提升约 26-27 个百分点（例如 DeepSeek-v3.2 57.8→84.9），且增加自动生成 rubric 的数量只带来递减/饱和收益，而增加 human rubric 数量单调提升。作为诊断（§5），他们报告生成 rubric 对 gold rubric 的覆盖率很低：Rubric Recall 仅 26.3%-53.8%（TICK 26.3、RocketEval 35.4、OpenRubric 47.5、Auto-Rubric 40.4、CheckEval 53.8），同时 Hallucination Rate 高达 54.1%-76.2%；5 个生成器中每个都是单流水线、各自生成，没有做跨生成器的并集/互补分析。
evidence_quote: models sustain high Hallucination Rates ( _>_ 70%) while missing nearly half of the critical constraints.
mismatch_note: 这是 D1 最直接的构念重合：Rubric Recall 就是『single-rub 对 golden-rub 准则集合的覆盖率』，数值上支持 H1(a)（覆盖率显著<1，且跨 5 个生成器系统性地低）。但差别有三：(1) 它把覆盖率当作 §5 的『诊断指标』，论文主张的构念/卖点是下游判别精度差（Rubric Gap），其余指标仅 'used only for diagnosis and ablations'（§4.1 L197）；(2) 只测单生成器 vs gold，未测不同 single-rub 之间的重叠/互补（H1b），也未测多 rubric 并集是否 > max(single) 及饱和上限（H1c）；(3) gold 被直接当作完整真值，未审计专家 rubric 本身是否穷尽。因此 P1(a) 的新颖性被它吃掉，P2/P3 未被覆盖。

their_construct: RubricRAG：在 HealthBench（医师撰写 instance-specific rubric）与 ResearchRubrics 两个 benchmark 上，令 Qwen3-14B 按 query 生成带正/负分值的 rubric，对比 zero-shot、random few-shot、retrieval(RubricRAG)、SFT、GRPO。覆盖/一致性由三类 set 级指标度量：Rubric-BLEU/Rubric-ROUGE/Rubric-LLM-Judge（macro 平均的 per-criterion best-overlap，双向 P/R/F1）、Missed@τ（reference rubric 中未被任何生成项覆盖的比例）、Hallucinations@τ、Redundancy@τ。下游再加：judge 用生成 rubric 与 gold rubric 各自打分后的 query 级相关、以及好/坏响应判别。
their_finding: off-the-shelf LLM zero-shot 生成的 rubric 与人类撰写 rubric 对齐很差：Missed@0.2 = 0.564（即 56.4% 的参考 rubric 项没有被覆盖），Hallucinations@0.2 = 0.557；用相似 query 检索作 exemplar（RubricRAG）可把 Missed@0.2 降到 0.412、Hallucinations@0.2 降到 0.416，但冗余上升。作者结论是『LLM 只抓到高层意图，无法复现 human rubric 中细粒度、领域扎根的准则』。
evidence_quote: we observe that using off-the-shelf LLMs result in poor rubric generators in the zero-shot setting.
mismatch_note: 构念与 P1(a) 高度重合：Missed@τ 的原文定义就是『the fraction of reference rubrics that are not sufficiently covered by any generated rubric』(L221)，即 1−覆盖率。它与 RubricBench 独立地给出了 single-generator 覆盖率<1 的证据（τ=0.2 时覆盖率仅 43.6%，τ=0.1 时则高达 95.1%——阈值极敏感，见 L366 表）。差别：(1) 只在医学/科研两个域、单一生成器 Qwen3-14B，未扫多模型；(2) 只有改善单条 rubric（检索/RAG）的动机，完全没有多 rubric 组装、跨 rubric 互补性/重叠、并集增益与上限的分析（P2/P3 空白）；(3) 仍把人类 rubric 当完整真值。

their_construct: GER-Eval：让 LLM 在 4 个数据集（HelpSteer2、SummEval、SumPubMed、USR）上、按 task 描述生成 5-8 条（每数据集，非 per-instance）rubric，再让模型用自生成或人类 rubric 打分。『覆盖/一致性』被操作化为 Align.(%)：用 GPT-4o 作 tagger，对每条生成准则标注其覆盖到的人类 rubric 项；若一条生成准则匹配不到任何人类项则记为 unseen，Align.=100×(1−#unseen/#unique)。即方向是『生成的准则有多少能映射到人类准则』（precision/幻觉的补），不是『人类准则有多少被生成准则覆盖』（recall）。模型：GPT-4o、GPT-4o-mini、Mixtral-8x22B、Llama-3.3-70B、Qwen2.5-72B。
their_finding: 模型生成的 rubric 大多能映射到人类 rubric 维度（Align.% 在多数数据集 >80%，HelpSteer2 最高 100%）；但该对齐在事实/知识密集任务（SumPubMed）显著下降（常 <60%），跨模型呈『模型内一致、模型间碎片化』。下游打分的可靠性在事实性场景退化。
evidence_quote: measures the proportion of generated criteria that can be mapped to a human-defined rubric
mismatch_note: 关键陷阱：方向是反的。Align.% 度量『生成项 → 人类项的映射率』，等于 1−hallucination（precision 视角），而我们的覆盖是『人类项 → 生成项的命中率』（recall）。因此它看似给出『LLM rubric 与人类 >80% 对齐』、像是反证 P1，实则完全不同构念，不得用作反对 P1 的证据。另有两点差异：(1) rubric 粒度是 per-dataset（5-8 条覆盖整个数据集），远粗于我们的 per-task instance rubric；(2) 无多模型组装、无互补性分析。只能作为『生成 rubric 存在幻觉/不可映射项』的旁证。

their_construct: SVR（Support Vector Rubrics）：把 rubric 构造重构为偏好对上的 max-margin 边界学习——从偏好对中对比式挖掘全局 rubric bank，学习 prompt-conditioned selector 与全局权重，用 support-pair 挖掘与对抗 hard-negative 迭代扩充/prune，测试时仅凭 prompt 检索 top-k rubric。评测主体是在 RubricBench 上的 pairwise accuracy，与 human-rubric oracle 对照；另在 RewardBench 1&2、RM-Bench 上验证。互补性只在『per-example 判别正确性』层面统计重叠（Table 5：both correct 69.6%、SVR-only 13.3%、oracle-only 13.5%、both wrong 3.7%）。
their_finding: self-generated rubric 在 RubricBench 上显著落后于 human-rubric oracle（引述 RubricBench：固定 judge 下人类 rubric 提升 >20 个百分点且跨 backbone 稳定，L17）；SVR 把与 oracle 的差距从 24.1 缩到 0.3（82.8 vs 83.1），且其与 oracle 在 26.8% 的样本上判断不同、各自唯一正确约 13%。作者将此归因于『目标错位』：自生成 rubric 在描述好答案，而非在判别边界附近区分候选。
evidence_quote: shows the two sources disagree on $26.8\%$ of them, with each uniquely correct on roughly $13\%$
mismatch_note: 纯下游判别精度研究（pairwise accuracy），不是准则级覆盖/互补测量。其 Table 5 的『互补性』是样例级判别结果的重叠（同一 pair 谁判对），与我们 H1b 的『不同 rubric 覆盖的准则集合之间的重叠率』是不同层面的量，不能混同。它对本子域的价值在于：(a) 独立复述并接受『rubric gap 存在』这一前提（说明 P1 现象的显著性已是社区共识、方法论文已在此前提上展开），(b) 提示 rubric 数量增加会饱和（bank 从 19→52→86、规模约 1023，属『reorganisation rather than expansion』L68），此点与 H1c 的上限相关但非同一构念。

their_construct: RRD：递归 decompose-filter 的 rubric 精炼框架。动机陈述里明确列出 rubric 生成的通病：『lack coverage, conflate dimensions, misalign preference direction, and contain redundant or highly correlated criteria』。但实际评测构念是下游：JudgeBench/PPE 上的 preference-judgment accuracy（GPT-4o、Llama3.1-405B judge），以及作为 RFT reward 时的 reward 增益与下游 BiGGen/HealthBench-Hard 迁移。未定义或测量 rubric 对参考/专家 rubric 的覆盖率。
their_finding: RRD 在 JudgeBench 上把 GPT-4o 的判准从 55.6% 提到 73.3%（+17.7 点），Llama-3.1-405B +6.6 点；作为 reward 使 RFT 的 reward 提升最多 160%（Qwen3-4B）/60%（Llama3.1-8B），远高于 10-20% 的基线。另观察到 rubric 数量从平均 7.4 增长并在约 20 处饱和。
evidence_quote: improves GPT-4o's accuracy from $55.6\%$ to $73.3\%$ ($+17.7$ points)
mismatch_note: 『rubrics often lack coverage…』只是 intro 的动机断言（main.tex:L181），全文没有把 coverage 操作化，也没有对专家 rubric 做覆盖率测量——所有收益都用下游判准/奖励衡量。因此不能算作『测过覆盖缺口』，只能算间接支持（rubric 生成确实不完整，故需精炼）。它的 rubric 数量饱和（7.4→~20）与 H1c 的『存在上限』形似而神不同：那是递归精炼的迭代饱和，不是多模型组装的覆盖率上限。

their_construct: 研究报告：在 TOEFL11 议论文评分（专家三档评级）上，比较三种 prompt 条件的下游一致性——完整 rubric（TOEFL 原版 375 词）、简化 rubric（78 词）、无 rubric——用 4 个模型（Claude 3.5 Haiku、Gemini 1.5 Flash、GPT-4o-mini、Llama 3 70B Instruct），指标为 QWK（与专家评分的二次加权 kappa）+ token 用量。rubric 均为人类撰写，非 LLM 生成；无覆盖度量。
their_finding: 4 个模型中 3 个在简化 rubric 下保持与完整 rubric 相近的评分准确率；Gemini 1.5 Flash 在更详细 rubric 下反而下降。结论是：多数 LLM-AES 应用里简化 rubric 可能足够，详细 rubric 并非必要，但模型间差异需逐一评估。
evidence_quote: three out of four models maintained similar scoring accuracy with the simplified rubric compared to the detailed one
mismatch_note: 构念差得最远：测的是『人类撰写的 rubric 详细程度』对下游 QWK 的影响，既非 LLM 生成了 rubric，也完全没有测量『覆盖了专家标准的多少准则』。它常被误读成『rubric 越全越好不成立』从而威胁 H1，但 QWK 对覆盖率不敏感（下游打分是粗粒度、可被少数强准则驱动），不能据此推断覆盖面不重要。且单任务（议论文评分）、专家 rubric 未公开，样本受限。归为 orthogonal，只作为『下游指标≠覆盖指标』的反面教材。

their_construct: Generating and Refining Dynamic Evaluation Rubrics for LLM-as-a-Judge（W7163068252）：无人工标注地自动生成 dataset-specific 与 instance-specific 细粒度 rubric，并用 meta-judge 偏好信号迭代微调 rubric 生成器。评测是四个 benchmark 上的 pairwise human agreement / pointwise Spearman-Pearson 相关，以及相对 human-crafted rubric（含 BiGGen instance-specific oracle 上界）的差距。无 rubric 覆盖率度量。
their_finding: 训练-free 的自动 rubric 生成在各 benchmark 上与现有方法大致相当；微调后的 14B rubric 生成器在 pairwise 与 pointwise 上超过所有现有基线，并缩小了与 oracle human-crafted rubric（BiGGen instance-specific）的差距。
evidence_quote: The fine-tuned generator consistently outperforms all existing methods and narrows the gap to oracle human-crafted rubrics.
mismatch_note: 下游对齐度研究（human agreement / 相关系数），『缩小了与 oracle rubric 的差距』指的是打分结果层面的差距，不是准则覆盖层面。它对 H1(a) 只能作间接旁证（存在与 oracle 的差距），不能作覆盖率证据；也没有多 rubric 组装或互补性实验（生成器是单一 Qwen3 14B 微调）。与 RubricBench/SVR 同属『把 rubric gap 当下游指标』的一类。

their_construct: Trains a query→rubric generator (Qwen3-4B/8B/14B) by RL. 'Multi-rubric' = n=8 rubric groups independently sampled from the SAME policy per query, used ONLY as a training-time cross-evaluation signal: r_comp(R_i) = mean over R_j of normalized score of the response induced by R_i. Quality is measured behaviourally — whether the response ranking induced by a generated rubric agrees with the ranking induced by the EXPERT-written rubric: Spearman rho, Kendall tau_b, Top-1, pairwise accuracy, over 700 expert-rubric queries (HealthBench 300, PRBench Finance/Legal 150+150, ResearchRubrics 100), 8 fixed response models, Qwen3.5-27B as criterion judge. No criterion-set coverage or overlap metric is defined.
their_finding: Best model GenRubric-14B reaches rho=0.4568, tau_b=0.3698, Top-1=0.3628, pairwise=0.6091 (GenRubric-8B best on Top-1 0.3761), above GPT-5.2 (rho=0.4343), Kimi-K2.5 (0.3670) and prior rubric generators (RubricRM-8B rho=0.2606). RL with r_comp alone lifts rho 0.324→0.438; full objective 0.452. Authors report a positive association between rubric 'coverage' and evaluation agreement, but coverage is only proxied by rubric LENGTH, never by matching criteria to the expert rubric.
evidence_quote: principle. Independently sampled rubric groups can be viewed as partial and noisy observations of the latent evaluation requirements of the same query. If $R_i$ is comprehensive, the response induced by it should not only satisfy its own criteria, but also satisfy complementary requirements captured by other sampled rubric groups.
mismatch_note: Direct conceptual neighbour but NOT our construct. (1) The 'multi' is type (i): repeated sampling of one policy, and only at TRAINING time; at inference GenRubric emits a single rubric. There is no multi-model/multi-perspective assembly. (2) The complementarity of independently sampled rubrics is the motivating PREMISE, never measured — no overlap/Jaccard/union-coverage statistic appears anywhere. (3) Ground truth is the expert rubric but the metric is downstream rank agreement (Spearman/Top-1), i.e. a behavioural proxy, not criterion-set coverage; the paper itself conflates 'coverage' with rubric length. So it constrains the novelty of our motivating premise and of the 'consensus over complementary rubrics' idea, but not of our measurement.

their_construct: MRRG: a single LLM writes 3-7 binary criteria (weight 1-3) under M=5 fixed prompt roles (User, Domain Expert, Educator, AI Researcher, Linguist); lists are concatenated and exact-match deduplicated; score = weighted sum of binary verdicts. Evaluated as pairwise preference validator on RewardBench-2 / JudgeBench / PPE with Qwen2.5-3B/7B/32B and gpt-oss-20b/120b, and as GRPO reward with a Qwen2.5-3B policy on BiGGen Bench and HealthBench-Hard. Explicit ablations: each single role alone; RSVRG = the same single-voiced prompt repeated 5 times + identical dedup pipeline; leave-one-role-out.
their_finding: On Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, MRRG scores 51.2 / 55.1 (RewardBench-2 / JudgeBench) versus the best single role (Educator) 37.8 / 44.8 and RSVRG w/ SR 43.9 / 45.1 — gaps of 7.3 and 10.0 points over repeated single-voiced sampling. Removing any one role changes performance only moderately. A t-SNE shows role rubrics cover single-voiced regions plus additional regions. Authors conclude the gains come from role-based diversity, not from generating more criteria.
evidence_quote:
This indicates that simply generating more single-voiced
rubrics cannot fully substitute for explicitly eliciting rubrics from
multiple complementary roles.
mismatch_note: Closest existing test of P2/P3, but the construct is shifted. (1) 'Multi' is type (ii)-lite: multiple ROLE PROMPTS on the SAME backbone model, not multiple models; our 'multi-model' comparison is untested. (2) The only novelty-relevant numbers are DOWNSTREAM pairwise accuracy on preference benchmarks, not coverage of a golden-rub criteria set; there is no ground-truth expert rubric and no criterion-level matching. (3) No overlap/redundancy rate between rubrics is reported (dedup is exact string match only), so H1b (low overlap) is neither measured nor refuted. (4) There is no scaling curve over the number of roles (only leave-one-out), so the H1c upper-bound clause is untested. (5) The repeated-sampling control (RSVRG) uses the SAME prompt 5×; that is a weaker control than our 'different models' condition.

their_construct: GER-Eval decouples rubric generation from rubric application. Five models (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Mixtral-8x22B, Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen2.5-72B) generate rubrics under 3 prompting conditions on 4 tasks (USR, SummEval, SumPubMed, HelpSteer2). Criterion-level metrics: Breadth (number of criteria), Unique% (percent not repeated), and Align.% = percentage of unique generated criteria that map to a human-defined rubric criterion. It then applies self-, human-, and other-model rubrics and measures zero-shot vs few-shot agreement and Spearman correlation with human scores, plus cross-model rubric transfer (ICC, Krippendorff alpha).
their_finding: Align.% exceeds 80 on most datasets (SumPubMed often <60); internal zero/few-shot consistency is 70-90%; correlation with human scores is rho≈0.8-0.9 on HelpSteer2/USR but ≈0.5 on SummEval and <0.3 on SumPubMed. Cross-model rubric transfer is the weakest condition (SumPubMed ICC<0.2, rho<0.3). Conclusion: models interpret their own rubrics best, human rubrics moderately, other models' rubrics least consistently — each model develops a distinct 'evaluation dialect', internally coherent but externally misaligned.
evidence_quote: Across all analyses, models interpret their own evaluation rubrics most effectively, human rubrics moderately well, and other models’ rubrics least consistently.
mismatch_note: The best methodological template in this subdomain for CRITERION-LEVEL comparison to a golden rubric, but the metric direction is wrong for us: Align.% is precision (fraction of GENERATED criteria that map to a human criterion), not recall (fraction of HUMAN criteria covered). It also never forms a UNION of different models' rubrics, so it gives no assembly gain and no complementarity number; divergence across models is inferred from transfer/consistency, not from set overlap. Ground truth is the datasets' human rubrics, but only 3-8 criteria per task, far coarser than HealthBench/RubricBench-style atomic criteria.

their_construct: Support Vector Rubrics: a global bank of 1,024 contrastively mined criteria plus a prompt-conditioned selector and learned weights; at inference the top-k rubrics are retrieved from the prompt alone. Compared against a human-rubric oracle on RubricBench (1,147 expert-annotated atomic-rubric pairs) by accuracy and by a per-example 2x2 correctness overlap table.
their_finding: SVR scores 82.8 vs the oracle's 83.1 on RubricBench, yet the two disagree on 26.8% of examples, with SVR uniquely correct on 13.3% and the oracle uniquely correct on 13.5%; the paper reads this as reaching oracle accuracy 'through a different set of decisions'. Case analysis attributes SVR misses to the absence of a 'did-the-response-perform-the-task' criterion, and oracle misses to over-weighting surface specifics.
evidence_quote: Table~\ref{tab:error_overlap} crosses per-example correctness on the $1{,}147$ pairs and shows the two sources disagree on $26.8\%$ of them, with each uniquely correct on roughly $13\%$.
mismatch_note: This is complementarity between ONE systematically-mined rubric source and the human oracle, not between multiple independently generated LLM rubrics. The unit is the per-example VERDICT (correct/wrong on a preference pair), not the criterion set, so it is evidence that different rubric sources 'see different things' but not evidence about criterion overlap rates or union coverage. No multi-model assembly is performed and no golden-rub coverage is computed (only downstream accuracy). Useful as motivation for P2 and as a precedent for reporting a 2x2 disagreement table.

their_construct: CalibratedRubric assembles a compact rubric bank from a candidate pool: Beta-Bernoulli measurability filtering, then an IRT model where each rubric is a test item, then IIF-Greedy selection maximizing a concave submodular 'information-coverage' utility over an ability grid. Evaluated by cross-fitted rank fidelity (Spearman AUC against the full response block) and by how many rubrics are needed to reach a target correlation of .95, on FinResearchBench, JudgmentBench, HealthBench and HelloBench.
their_finding: Greedy coverage assembly beats random selection in all six blocks; reaching the target correlation needs 28 rather than 51 rubrics for evidence reasoning and 49 rather than 131 for decision support; across the other blocks 43-273 items versus 142-1,226 under random selection. The gain over plain information ranking is significant only in the two larger 15-system blocks, which the authors describe as supporting the coverage mechanism 'most clearly at the larger leaderboard size, not a universal advantage'.
evidence_quote:
Our final assembler instead optimizes the concave information-coverage
utility
mismatch_note: A homonym trap: 'coverage' here is TEST-INFORMATION coverage over an IRT ability range, i.e. how well a rubric set separates model ability levels — not coverage of a golden rubric's criteria. It is also subset SELECTION/COMPRESSION from one existing pool, not the union of independently generated rubrics; there is no notion of complementary perspectives and no golden-rub. Its '49 vs 131' is a compression budget, not an assembly upper bound, so it does not answer H1c. Listed because it is the only work with an explicit submodular coverage objective that could be borrowed as a formalization, and because naive keyword search for 'coverage' will over-count it.

their_construct: RubricAtlas mines type-level rubrics (recurring analytical questions) from 3,079 expert Chinese financial reports across 99 research types, then measures how much of a type's question set is supported by k reference reports: median/mean coverage per single report, leave-one-out, half-pool, and k=1/3/10 curves; plus deletion and padding perturbations on re-scored reports.
their_finding: A single report covers only 51% (k=1 type mean; 54% median across reports; 57% for task-source reports); leave-one-out 53%, half-out 56%; k=3 reports cover 79% and k=10 cover 96% of the type atlas. About ten reports recover much of the full pool's coverage, which the authors call an internal planning reference rather than a sufficiency threshold. Source subsets shift completeness by a measurable amount and change the task-level leader on 24% of tasks at k=1.
evidence_quote: A single report thus represents only part of a type's recurring analyses, even excluding its contribution to question selection.
mismatch_note: The closest existing measurement DESIGN to H1a+H1c — a coverage curve over independent sources with a union/saturation point — but the sources are EXPERT REPORTS, not LLM-generated rubrics, and there is no multi-model LLM element. Coverage is defined over a type-level question set (a superset reference), which is exactly the golden-rub-style denominator we need, but the reference set is itself machine-extracted from expert documents. Treat as a protocol template (denominator construction, k-curve, leave-one-out/half-out controls, deletion vs padding controls), not as evidence about LLM rubrics.

their_construct: CDRRM: contrastive profiling of preference pairs followed by rubric synthesis, then a trained Rubric Generator and a rubric-conditioned Judge Model. Evaluated on RewardBench, RMBench and RMB. It contains a perturbation study that masks 1-3 rubrics (with rationales) from the >=7 generated rubrics per sample and retrains the reward model.
their_finding: Masking 1-3 generated rubrics changes accuracy by at most 0.42% (95.65 baseline -> 95.23 / 95.37), which the authors read as showing that a significant portion of generated rubrics in current datasets is redundant rather than informative.
evidence_quote: This finding confirms that a significant portion of the generated rubrics in current datasets creates non-trivial redundancy rather than providing informative signals.
mismatch_note: The redundancy measured is WITHIN a single generated rubric set (ablating items of one rubric), not overlap BETWEEN two independently generated rubrics, so it does not directly refute H1b. But it is the strongest caution in this round: if within-rubric items are already highly redundant, then two independently generated rubrics from the same model family may overlap heavily and the 'complementarity' in H1b could be small. Our design must therefore separate within-rubric redundancy from cross-rubric overlap, and must control for rubric length/verbosity. No golden-rub coverage is measured; metric is preference accuracy.

their_construct: Measures 'rubric interference': one judge model, response fixed, compares per-rubric verdicts when rubrics are evaluated in isolation vs jointly; four controlled operations (set expansion, subsetting, reordering, noise injection). Datasets: HealthBench (binary), FLASK and ResearchQA (scored); model families Qwen3 and Llama-3.1; metrics are per-rubric agreement, mean absolute deviation (MAD), and sample-level exact match.
their_finding: Going from isolation to a joint pass gives only 36% sample-level exact match for Qwen3-32B on HealthBench (>=0.98 self-agreement across seeds, so it is systematic). MAD grows with the number of co-evaluated rubrics K: Qwen3-32B goes from .203 at K=2 to .362 at K=8. Reordering rubrics alone can flip a verdict. They train SARA to restore isolation-like verdicts.
evidence_quote:
Figure~\ref{fig:con_k} traces MAD on ResearchQA as $K$ grows
from 2 to 8. For all base models, MAD rises steeply with $K$:
Qwen3-32B climbs from .203 at $K{=}2$ to .362 at $K{=}8$,
nearly doubling.
mismatch_note: Orthogonal in construct but a hard practical constraint for us: it shows that evaluating an assembled multi-rubric jointly in one judge pass degrades per-criterion verdicts as the rubric set grows. It says nothing about rubric CONTENT coverage, overlap or assembly gain. Implication for our protocol: score criteria in isolation (one call per criterion) or use SARA-style anchoring, otherwise any measured H1c 'ceiling' may be a judge-interference artifact rather than a coverage ceiling.

their_construct: Document-grounded automatic rubric construction for M&A due diligence: 16 development + 4 held-out tasks. Five complementary generation processes (free-form generation plus obligation / entity cross-reference / fact-to-schedule search axes) populate a candidate pool; coverage is macro recall of criteria in the senior-authored reference rubric under an LLM-based criterion-equivalence protocol. Baseline includes strong single-call GPT generation.
their_finding: Multi-axis generation raises held-out family-average reference recall from 0.782 (GPT single-call) to 0.872; the measured full candidate-pool ceiling is 0.876, i.e. recall < 1. At selection budget k=60 the deployable reference-free ranker recovers only 0.349 recall vs 0.876 for the reference-informed diagnostic (a 52.7-point coverage-selection gap).
evidence_quote: new structural axes add +0.060 to +0.100 recall, while volume expansions add at most +0.015.
mismatch_note: Closest existing measurement of generated-rubric coverage against an expert rubric (recall<1) and of volume saturation. But: single domain (M&A due diligence); a single generator family plus a document-search pipeline rather than independent single-model rubrics; criterion equivalence judged by an LLM in the same model family (not human); no cross-rubric overlap/union beyond one pairwise union; 'volume expansion' means more sampling along existing axes, not adding more independently generated rubrics.

their_construct: Complementarity test on fixed held-out candidate pools: compares recall against the senior-authored reference rubric for the union of two independently produced rubric sets (GPT single-call generation vs the authors' multi-axis pipeline) on the two tasks with complete shared outputs.
their_finding: The union reaches 0.934 macro recall vs 0.829 for GPT alone and 0.895 for the multi-axis pipeline alone. The authors interpret the gain as evidence that even strong generators miss different requirements, and recommend mechanisms for identifying novel marginal coverage instead of resampling a single view.
evidence_quote: The union gain shows that even strong generators miss different requirements; it also suggests that future work should emphasize mechanisms for identifying novel marginal coverage rather than repeatedly sampling a single search view.
mismatch_note: This is a union of two heterogeneous systems, not N i.i.d. single rubrics from several model families; no per-criterion overlap/Jaccard, no marginal-gain-vs-number-of-rubrics curve (one union point only), and only two tasks. It demonstrates complementarity but not the systematic cross-model overlap structure our H1(b) asks about.

their_construct: Training-free, reference-free multi-role rubric generation: five fixed roles (User, Domain Expert, Educator, AI Researcher, Linguist) are elicited from the SAME backbone LLM, pooled, weighted and deduplicated into one rubric. Evaluated by downstream pairwise judging accuracy on RewardBench-2 / JudgeBench / PPE and by GRPO-style RLVR. Key control: RSVRG = five repeated single-voiced generations passed through the identical post-processing.
their_finding: MRRG beats the single-voiced baselines (SVRG w/o and w/ sampled responses, CtT) by 3.1-16.4 points; any single role is 10-13 points worse than MRRG; and RSVRG (repeated single-voiced sampling, same post-processing) still trails MRRG by 7.3 points on RewardBench-2 and 10.0 on JudgeBench. Authors conclude the gains come from role/perspective diversity rather than from producing more criteria.
evidence_quote: This indicates that simply generating more single-voiced rubrics cannot fully substitute for explicitly eliciting rubrics from multiple complementary roles.
mismatch_note: No coverage/overlap measurement against any expert golden rubric; the 'dimensional blind spots' claim rests on downstream accuracy plus a qualitative case study, and on equal-criterion-count controls only indirectly. Roles are prompt-conditioned instances of one backbone model, not different models, so this is evidence about perspective diversity, not about multi-model complementarity. Measures only downstream scoring, which is indirect evidence for our construct.

their_construct: Training-free rubric generation at two granularities (dataset-specific and instance-specific, generated from the query only, no reference answers), followed by an optional DPO fine-tune of a generator using a strong meta-judge's pairwise preferences over rubric candidates. Evaluated on HelpSteer2, BiGGen, AlpacaEval, MT-Bench by judge-human agreement / correlation; BiGGen supplies human-crafted instance rubrics as an oracle.
their_finding: The training-free generator is competitive with or superior to existing methods on AlpacaEval and HelpSteer2; instance-specific rubrics beat dataset-specific for every judge; human-crafted instance-specific rubrics still outperform all automated methods by a large margin. DPO iterations give small but consistent gains (+1.15 then +1.53 points).
evidence_quote: Human-crafted instance-specific rubrics (available only for \textsc{BiGGen}) further outperform all automated methods by a large margin (78.33\% vs.\ 74.82\%, 0.584 vs.\ 0.454 with Claude Sonnet 4),
mismatch_note: Measures downstream judge-human agreement, not criterion-set coverage against the expert rubric; the 'expert rubrics win' result is only an indirect proxy for incomplete coverage. One judge model both generates and judges; no multi-model comparison and no overlap analysis. The instance-vs-dataset contrast is a granularity axis, not a coverage axis.

their_construct: Contrastive Rubric Generation (CRG): from (prompt, chosen, rejected) preference pairs, derive hard rules (explicit constraints) and principles (implicit qualities), keep rubrics passing a preference-label consistency filter, then train a rubric-generation model and a rubric-conditioned reward model (Rubric-RM). Evaluated by reward-model preference accuracy (e.g. RM-Bench, HealthBench), not by criterion coverage against expert rubrics.
their_finding: Rubric-RM surpasses strong size-matched baselines by 8.4% on average; contrastive, domain-tuned rubric training beats on-the-fly direct prompting substantially (direct Qwen-3-8B Rubric+Judge pipeline scores 51.8 on HealthBench vs RUBRIC-RM's +16.5).
evidence_quote: Directly prompting Qwen-3-8B with a Rubric+Judge pipeline yields only 51.8, whereas RUBRIC-RM improves performance by **+16.5** .
mismatch_note: Requires labeled preference pairs and training; contrastive criteria are selected to discriminate the observed response pairs, so criterion coverage is inherited from the annotation/response distribution (GenRubric makes exactly this critique). Pure downstream accuracy, no golden-rub coverage metric. Included as the reference implementation of the 'contrastive generation' baseline class, not as evidence about our H.

their_construct: Recursive decompose-filter rubric refinement, training-free at inference (LLM calls, no human labels): decompose any criterion satisfied by more than two rollouts, filter misaligned criteria (those that favor a weaker model) and redundant/overlapping criteria, then assign whitened correlation-aware weights. Evaluated by JudgeBench / PPE judge accuracy and by reward quality during RFT.
their_finding: JudgeBench accuracy for GPT-4o rises 55.6 -> 73.3 (+17.7); the rubric set grows from 7.4 and plateaus at about 20 by iteration 3, and the loop stops once proposals stop being novel/valid/non-redundant (termination threshold on rejected proposals).
evidence_quote: We repeat this decomposition--filtering loop until the proposer struggles to produce novel, valid, non-redundant items.
mismatch_note: No expert golden rubric: 'coverage' is a design desideratum operationalized only as judge accuracy. The saturation is a heuristic stopping rule, not a measured coverage-vs-rubric-count curve, and recursion re-decomposes one initial set rather than adding independent rubrics. Also reports (secondary) that a GPT-4o proposer benefits more from Gemini-generated sample responses than its own — a complementarity hint, but downstream-only.

their_construct: Self-evolving RL for rubric generation from unlabeled queries: sample n rubric groups per query, induce responses conditioned on each rubric, then cross-evaluate every induced response with every other rubric group (cross-rubric comprehensiveness) plus group- and criterion-level rewards. Models at 4B/8B/14B. Evaluated by agreement (Spearman, Kendall tau-b, Top-1, pairwise) between evaluations induced by generated vs expert-written rubrics on human-annotated rubric benchmarks.
their_finding: GenRubric beats specialized rubric generators and general-purpose LLMs across model sizes and on held-out domains; the authors report that longer/more comprehensive rubrics associate positively with evaluation agreement, while length alone is not sufficient.
evidence_quote: The results also indicate a positive association between rubric coverage and evaluation agreement, although length alone is not sufficient to guarantee strong performance.
mismatch_note: Coverage is inferred through induced-evaluation agreement, never measured as recall of expert rubric criteria. Requires RL training (not training-free) and many LLM calls per query; compares against expert rubrics at the level of induced rankings, not criterion sets. Does not compare N independent single rubrics across model families nor measure their overlap. Included as the 'online/self-evolution' baseline class.

their_construct: Offline Coarse-to-Fine rubric data pipeline: (1) principle-guided and response-grounded rubric synthesis, (2) multi-model aggregation — parallel candidate sets from heterogeneous frontier models (e.g. GPT-5.1, Gemini 3 Pro Preview) merged into a unified pool and distilled to one compact base rubric via an aggregation prompt, (3) difficulty evolution. Produces ~110k (query, rubric) pairs; validated only by downstream post-training scores (HealthBench, LLMEval-Med).
their_finding: Ablation on HealthBench: naive single-model generation 60.9 -> +principle/response grounding 63.8 -> +multi-model aggregation 65.0 -> +difficulty evolution 66.2; the authors attribute the multi-model gain to mitigating single-model 'perspective bias' (blind spots / narrow standards).
evidence_quote: Individual models often exhibit inherent blind spots and subjective preferences, yielding narrow standards that fail to recognize valid responses with distinct presentations.
mismatch_note: This is the closest existing 'multi-rub' construction: heterogeneous models generate candidate criteria then are merged into ONE compact rubric. But it is an offline, compute-heavy, multi-model distillation pipeline evaluated only by downstream task scores; aggregation deliberately collapses diversity, so complementarity/overlap and the 'union vs max single' question are never measured. No golden-rub coverage metric.

their_construct: Meta-evaluation of LLM-authored rubrics for PaperBench (ML paper reproduction) across four incrementally augmented generation settings (direct prompting -> in-context examples -> agentic scaffolding -> distilled procedural skill) and three backbones (Claude-Sonnet, GPT-5.4, DeepSeek-V4-Pro). Intrinsic: semantic/lexical similarity and matching precision/recall/F1 against ground-truth expert rubrics (embedding cosine). Extrinsic: correlation of induced repository scores with PaperBench.
their_finding: Augmentation improves recall-driven coverage and F1 (e.g. DeepSeek-V4-Pro F1 0.49 -> 0.70), and the strongest setting approaches the human extrinsic baseline (Spearman 0.78 vs 0.83). Yet generated rubrics remain overly fine-grained with lower recall and only modest intrinsic gains; the residual gap to human annotation is attributed to coverage and granularity.
evidence_quote: However, taken together with lower recall and longer rubrics in Table 1, this pattern indicates a tendency toward overly finegrained criteria, which limit models’ holistic coverage of the ground-truth rubric.
mismatch_note: The closest prior measurement of generated-rubric criterion coverage against an expert rubric across several backbones — a real novelty threat to P1. But: single domain (PaperBench paper reproduction); one rubric per setting per paper; the four settings are scaffolding augmentations, not independent multi-model sampling; matching is embedding cosine similarity rather than human/LLM equivalence; no overlap/complementarity analysis and no multi-rub assembly.

their_construct: Tests whether off-the-shelf LLMs generate instance-specific rubrics aligned with human-authored rubrics, across two rubric benchmarks and multiple prompting/post-training strategies; proposes RubricRAG, an inference-time retrieval of rubrics from related queries to supply domain knowledge.
their_finding: Off-the-shelf LLM-generated rubrics show limited alignment with human-written rubrics; retrieval of related rubrics improves both similarity to human rubrics and downstream LLM-judge accuracy.
evidence_quote: Across two rubric benchmarks and multiple prompting and post-training strategies, we find that off-the-shelf LLMs produce rubrics with limited alignment to human-written ones.
mismatch_note: Abstract-only: no arXiv version and the ACM DOI has no open PDF, so full text was not obtained. It broadly supports P1 but cannot be used for any key conclusion. It is a retrieval-augmented, inference-time method (a distinct baseline class from direct generation).

their_construct: First study of self-preference bias (SPB) under rubric-based evaluation. Binary verdict per criterion (single-rubric SR and all-rubrics AR) vs pairwise comparison (PWC) and direct assessment (DA). Ground truth: programmatic rubric verification on IFEval and LiveCodeBench; on HealthBench a majority vote of the largest judge per family (Gemma3-27B, Llama4-Maverick, Qwen3-235B, GPT-oss-120B, Claude Sonnet 4.5). Metric: rubric-level overestimation = P(judge marks failed rubric satisfied), aggregated into Harmful Self-Preference Propensity Ratio (HSPP-R_self / HSPP-R_fam) = own-overestimation / mean overestimation of unrelated models. Judges/generators: Gemma 3 27/12/4B, Llama 4 Maverick/Scout, Qwen 3 235/30/4B, GPT-5, GPT-oss-120B, Claude 4.5 Sonnet/Haiku.
their_finding: SPB persists in rubric-based evaluation even with fully objective, programmatically verifiable criteria and after stratifying by instance difficulty: for failed rubrics a judge can be >50% more likely to mark them passed when the output is its own; worst case GPT-5 20x own-vs-other overestimation on LiveCodeBench. RB is less biased than PWC and comparable to DA. Ensembling judges reduces but does not eliminate SPB. Mechanism audit: SPB correlates with self-recognition (HSPP 1.88 when own output recognised vs 0.72 when not on LiveCodeBench) and with output length, but NOT mainly with perplexity (HSPP remains 1.48 on LiveCodeBench and 1.03 on HealthBench in the lowest-perplexity quartile). Negative rubrics and communication/emergency-referral themes amplify SPB.
evidence_quote: We present the first study of SPB in rubric-based evaluation, an increasingly popular benchmarking paradigm where judges issue binary verdicts on individual evaluation criteria, instead of assigning holistic scores or rankings.
mismatch_note: Closest existing work to H2 and the one that most constrains its positioning, but NOT the same construct: the rubric is fixed by the benchmark and identical for every generator, so the judge never generates criteria and 'coverage of a golden rubric' is not a variable. It therefore measures verdict-level overestimation under a fixed instrument, not coverage/complementarity of model-generated rubrics. Crucially for H2 it already decomposes rival mechanisms (length, perplexity, self-recognition) at rubric level and finds residual SPB, so H2 must show coverage adds variance beyond these; however their setup cannot refute H2 because coverage is held constant across generators. Also note its perplexity conclusion contradicts record 2410.21819.

their_construct: Quantifies self-preference bias in pairwise dialogue evaluation using an Equal Opportunity fairness metric: Bias = P(judge prefers own | human prefers own) - P(judge prefers own | human does not), on 33k Chatbot Arena pairs with human preference labels. Eight evaluator models (GPT-4, GPT-3.5-Turbo, Vicuna-7b/13b, oasst-pythia-12b, dolly-v2-12b, Koala-13b, stablelm-tuned-alpha-7b). Mechanism test: bin pairs by within-pair log-perplexity difference and compare judge win-rate curves to human win-rate curves, split by whether the judge's own output is present.
their_finding: GPT-4 shows the largest SPB (0.520); Vicuna-13b and Koala-13b also significant; three models show reverse (negative) bias. LLM judges weight perplexity far more than humans: they give higher evaluations to lower-perplexity text regardless of authorship. Conditioned on perplexity, own vs non-own win rates are statistically indistinguishable for most models, and models' own outputs have lower average perplexity. The authors conclude SPB may be 'the model's own output inherently exhibits lower perplexity' (familiarity/perplexity explanation).
evidence_quote: This suggests that the factor influencing the LLM evaluators' judgments is not whether the response is their own but rather the perplexity of the responses.
mismatch_note: This is a rival mechanism, not a test of coverage: task is open-ended chat pairwise comparison on Chatbot Arena; no rubric and no criterion set, so rubric coverage is undefined. GPT-4/GPT-3.5 (the models with strongest SPB) could not be analysed for perplexity at all, and the study predates rubric-based judging. Its strong 'perplexity is the essence' claim is contradicted at rubric level by 2604.06996, so it should be treated as one candidate explanation of unknown generality rather than settled fact.

their_construct: Tests whether self-recognition capability causes self-preference. Summarization tasks (CNN/DailyMail, XSUM) with GPT-3.5-Turbo, GPT-4, Llama 2 as evaluators/generators; self-recognition measured as confidence-accuracy at identifying own vs other-LLM/human summaries (pairwise and individual settings); self-preference measured as Likert/pairwise score advantage for own summaries. Causal design: supervised fine-tuning on the self-recognition task raises/lowers recognition, then correlation with self-preference is measured; controls include fine-tuning on length, vowel count, readability, constant/random answers; label-swap (correct vs reversed authorship labels) experiment.
their_finding: Out of the box all three LLMs distinguish their own outputs at >50% accuracy (GPT-4 73.5%); fine-tuning reaches >90% recognition. Strength of self-preference is linearly correlated with self-recognition capability across fine-tuning conditions and datasets, and the correlation survives control fine-tuning tasks; reversing authorship labels reverses self-preference for GPT-4/GPT-3.5 on XSUM. The authors themselves caution the correlation does not prove the causal hypothesis.
evidence_quote: By fine-tuning LLMs, we discover a linear correlation between self-recognition capability and the strength of self-preference bias; using controlled experiments, we show that the causal explanation resists straightforward confounders.
mismatch_note: Competing mechanism (self-recognition), measured on single-document summarization with holistic preference, no evaluation criteria at all; it cannot speak to coverage of a golden rubric. The paper itself notes the causal claim is not fully validated (icml2024.tex:L344). Importantly, record 2604.06996 finds self-recognition is the strongest of the three output-property explanations specifically in rubric-based judging, making it the main rival H2 must beat on incremental variance.

their_construct: Style/format bias in judging. 40 general questions; GPT-4-generated answers deliberately perturbed along length, grammatical proficiency (advanced/intermediate English learner), and injected factual errors. Judges: crowd-sourced annotators, expert annotators, GPT-4, Claude-1; Elo ratings from pairwise judgments; inter-annotator kappa; checks whether length/grammar dominate factual correctness.
their_finding: All judges favour longer text, GPT-4 most and experts least. Judges sometimes prefer answers with factual errors over short or grammatically flawed correct answers; when GPT-4 fails to catch an inaccuracy it often favours the flawed long output. GPT-4/Claude-1 show position bias toward Assistant 1; humans are indecisive (narrow Elo range, more ties). Authors recommend multi-dimensional (Multi-Elo) evaluation.
evidence_quote: When the LLM fails to detect inaccuracies, it often favors flawed outputs over shorter or grammatically imprecise responses.
mismatch_note: Establishes a style/length/grammar weighting bias but NOT self-preference: all answers come from one generator (GPT-4) and the 'models' being ranked are style conditions, so authorship is not varied. No rubric, no criterion set, no coverage measurement. Useful to H2 as a competing 'judges weight surface style over substance' explanation that any coverage-based account must control for (length is also a confound in 2604.06996).

their_construct: Bias audit of LLM evaluators on SummEval summarization: GPT-4 (and GPT-3.5) assign 1-5 scores on coherence/consistency/fluency/relevance; compared with expert ratings. Familiarity bias operationalized as negative association between GPT-3 perplexity of the summary (and of the source document) and the evaluator's score, compared against the perplexity-score association for human experts. Also measures rating-distribution skew and anchoring in multi-attribute judgments.
their_finding: GPT-4 is disproportionately biased toward low-perplexity summaries relative to expert annotators: high-scored (5) summaries have lower mean perplexity than experts' high-scored ones. GPT-4 ratings are even negatively correlated with source-document perplexity where expert ratings show no correlation. The authors generalize self-enhancement bias into 'familiarity bias' (preference for text one is familiar with). They also report score-scale non-respect and anchoring.
evidence_quote: GPT-4 is disproportionately biased towards low perplexity summaries as compared with expert annotators.
mismatch_note: Rival mechanism (perplexity/familiarity). Ground truth is human holistic scores on four pre-defined summarization dimensions, not an expert rubric with per-criterion coverage; no self-preference condition (the judge is not the generator of the summaries). The causal reading is associational: lower perplexity could proxy fluency or quality. Summarization-only, GPT-4-centric.

their_construct: GER-Eval: decouples rubric generation from rubric application. Five LLMs (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Mixtral 8x22B, Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen2.5-72B) generate 5-8 criteria under three prompting conditions on USR, SummEval, SumPubMed, HelpSteer2, then apply their own vs human rubrics in zero/few-shot. Metrics: rubric breadth, uniqueness, Align. = percent of generated criteria that map to a human-defined rubric criterion, zero/few-shot score agreement, and Spearman correlation with human scores; cross-model rubric transfer (ICC/alpha/Fleiss kappa).
their_finding: LLM-generated rubrics are coherent and mostly map to human criteria (alignment typically >80% on several datasets, but below 60% on SumPubMed), yet scoring is reliable only within a model: zero/few-shot agreement is 70-90% within model, while cross-model agreement and alignment with human judgments are weaker. Rubrics are model-dependent ('consistent within models but fragmented across them'). Factual/knowledge-intensive settings degrade reliability. GPT-4o rubrics emphasize Depth/Creativity, Llama's Fluency/Contextual Understanding.
evidence_quote: These rubrics enable consistent scoring within models but exhibit limited cross-model agreement and weaker alignment with human judgments
mismatch_note: Nearest prior work on the H2 premise that different models select different evaluation criteria: it shows model-dependent rubric content and imperfect mapping to human criteria. But it measures only alignment/ranking correlation, never coverage of the full golden criterion set (a criterion can be 'aligned' while others are missing; breadth is only 5-8 criteria). It has no self-preference condition, no judge-as-generator design, and no criterion-level overlap analysis, so it does not test 'coverage difference causes bias'. For P1 it is a partial novelty threat because it already compares model-generated criteria against human rubrics.

their_construct: JudgeProfile decomposes LLM judging into perception (per-attribute pairwise judgments on 87 attributes) and prioritization (weights mapping attributes to the overall choice). 50,013 response pairs from 17 sources, 21 LLM judges; attribute weights fitted per judge from its own overall choices; reference labels used to learn new weights and test reweighting as steering.
their_finding: Judges often agree on attribute-level perception even when their overall winners diverge; fitted attribute weights differ substantially across judges even when estimated from the same attribute judgments, and are reproducible within judge. Reweighting perceived attributes raises held-out agreement with reference labels from 66.48% to 71.97%. Subjectivity therefore lives at least partly in criteria prioritization, not only perception.
evidence_quote: These weights differ across judges even when estimated from the same attribute judgments.
mismatch_note: Not a self-preference paper: authorship is not manipulated and self/family effects are not measured. It is relevant only as machinery/evidence that judges weight evaluation facets differently; it measures pairwise preference weights, not rubric coverage, and its 87 attributes are researcher-supplied rather than model-generated or expert-golden. Could serve as a methodological template for quantifying 'which facets a judge uses', but not as evidence for or against H2.

their_construct: Sanity check of self-preference measurements: re-baselines self-preferring verdicts against the judge's own voting distribution on cases where it evaluates itself vs another model (evaluator-quality null), across previous self-preference studies; compares entropy of voting distributions.
their_finding: Only 51% of examples in prior findings retain statistical significance against the evaluator-quality null, covering 89.6% of total self-preference probability mass; argues much apparent self-preference is confounded by evaluator quality/uncertainty rather than authorship.
evidence_quote: only 51% of examples in previous findings retain statistical significance against this null hypothesis, covering 89.6% of total self-preference probability mass.
mismatch_note: Abstract-only, not read in full; do not use as a conclusion basis. It measures the robustness of SPB estimates, not rubric coverage; if its critique holds it raises the bar for H2 by shrinking the amount of 'bias' left to explain. Must be read in full before citing, because it may materially change the baseline variance that H2 must add to.

their_construct: Statistical identification framework for self-bias: models the difference between the judge's score distribution on its own completions vs others', controlling for true quality via an independent third-party judge (humans). >5000 prompt-completion pairs, expert human annotations, nine LLM judges.
their_finding: GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet systematically assign higher scores to their own outputs; these models also show family-bias toward other models in the same family. The framework is designed to avoid conflating genuine quality differences with bias.
evidence_quote: These models also display family-bias; systematically assigning higher ratings to outputs produced by other models of the same family.
mismatch_note: Abstract-only, not read in full; used only as a pointer to the strongest current self/family-bias quantification. Pointwise scoring on human-annotated prompt-completion pairs, no rubric and no criterion coverage; it establishes that family-level bias is real but says nothing about which evaluation facets drive it. A full-text read is needed before using its effect sizes in an H2 baseline model.

their_construct: RubricBench：1,147 组 pairwise 比较，每组配一条专家标注的 atomic binary rubric（2–10 条 Yes/No，集中在 4–6 条），rubric 只从 instruction 推导、不看候选回答；9 名专家标注者，独立双标 + 资深评审合并（只保留共识项）；ground truth = 人工 rubric + 人工 preference label。覆盖度定义为 Rubric Recall = 被至少一条生成准则匹配上的人类准则数 / 人类准则总数，另报 Hallucination Rate 与 Structural F1；匹配由 Qwen3-30B-A3B 在严格语义等价口径下判定（匹配器 human-model 一致率 0.79、model-model 0.85）。被测对象包括 Auto-Rubric、RocketEval、CheckEval、TICK、OpenRubric 等 rubric-aware 生成器。
their_finding: 单生成器 rubric 对人类准则的结构性 recall 只有 26.3%–53.8%（最高 CheckEval 53.8%），hallucination rate 54.1%–76.2%，Structural F1 24.8–38.3；同一批 judge 用人工 rubric 时准确率 83–92%，换成生成 rubric 只有 54–61%；这个约 26% 的“Rubric Gap”在 GPT-OSS-120B、Gemini-3-Pro、Qwen3.5-Plus 等前沿模型上稳定存在，且 test-time 增加生成条数（Rub@4→@32）或迭代 refine 都不能收敛（GPT-4o-mini 48.0%→46.8%）。
evidence_quote: These results demonstrate that the primary bottleneck lies in rubric quality rather than evaluator reasoning ability. Even humans struggle when constrained by low-quality generated rubrics, confirming that rubric mis-specification is the dominant factor behind the observed Rubric Gap.
mismatch_note: 它已经在准则级测了“单 rubric 覆盖 < 1”，我们 P1(a) 的现象陈述不能再算新。但差距明确：(i) 只报每个生成器一个聚合均值，没有 per-instance 覆盖分布、没有按模型族/领域分层，无法支撑“不完整是系统性的”这一更强主张；(ii) rubric 来自既有 rubric-aware pipeline，不是“单个通用 LLM 直接写 rubric”，与我们的 single-rub 操作化不同；(iii) 完全没有跨模型/跨视角 rubric 的并集覆盖或重叠率（P2/P3），它的“增加条数”是同一生成器扩写，属冗余而非异质互补；(iv) 覆盖靠一个 LLM 语义匹配器，等价关系偏严格，绝对 recall 数值不宜直接搬用，只可复用法。

their_construct: HealthBench：5,000 段多轮医患对话，每段配一套 conversation-specific rubric；共 48,562 条唯一准则、median 11 条/例（2–48 条），由 262 名来自 60 国的医生撰写；准则写成自洽、客观、可二分判定的条目并带正负权重。另有 34 条预写 consensus criteria（全库出现 8,053 次），仅在 ≥2 名评审医生多数同意适用于该例时才挂上。ground truth 用于“判分”而非“写准则”：在 consensus 子集上收集医生对 (criterion, conversation, response) 的 met/not-met 标注，共 60,896 条 meta-example，用 Macro-F1 比较模型 grader 与医生。grader 为 GPT-4.1。
their_finding: GPT-4.1 作为 rubric grader 在 7 个主题中的 5 个超过医生平均 MF1、6/7 位于医生上半区、全部 7 个高于医生 33 分位；整体 MF1=0.709。医生自身加权 MF1 仅 0.569–0.730（按主题），个体医生差异很大。HealthBench Consensus 被明确描述为“更高医生验证、精度更高但 recall 更低、只抓很窄一类问题”的子集。
evidence_quote: It exceeds the average physician score in five out of seven themes, is in the upper half of physicians for six out of seven themes, and is above the lower third (33rd percentile) of physicians for all themes.
mismatch_note: 它是目前最可扩展的 golden-rub 来源（准则级、可枚举、专家写、带权重与正负号），但两个关键点与我们不同：(i) 一致性只测“应用已定准则”的 met/not-met 一致，从未测“两位医生独立会写出同一组准则”的一致，准则集本身被当作给定真值；(ii) 只有 34 条 consensus criteria 经过多医生共识，其余绝大多数准则由单名医生为该例撰写，作者的措辞也承认 consensus 子集是“高精度低 recall”。若我们拿 HealthBench 当 golden-rub，必须自己补一层“准则集完备性/可复现性”的假设检验。另：该 arXiv 记录未被 OpenAlex 索引，citation_count 无法取得，暂填 0（不代表实际影响力）。

their_construct: ResearchRubrics：101 个开放域 research prompt，每个配 20–43 条 prompt-specific 准则，共 2,593 条，2,800+ 小时人工。撰写采用三角色流水线：Expert 1 起草 prompt+准则，Expert 2 审阅并与 Expert 1 迭代至通过，Expert 3 独立终审修订；明示“没有任何准则由 LLM 生成或播种”。准则分 mandatory（权重 ±4/±5）与 optional（±1..±3），负权重惩罚错误。评测协议是 LLM-as-judge 对每条准则给 Satisfied/Partially/Not 三值，加权归一；人机一致性用 Macro-F1，9 名专家标注者对 303 条回答提供 ground truth。
their_finding: 二元化后 human–LLM judge Macro-F1 为 0.717–0.760（超过 HealthBench 的 0.709），三值化则掉到 0.527–0.567；给准则加具体例子可提升 3–4%，而用 LLM 自动扩写准则会灾难性下降 15–20%。最强 DR agent 对专家 rubric 的合规率仍低于 68%。
evidence_quote: The pipeline involves three experts, each assigned to a distinct and separate role. Expert 1 initially proposes a prompt and a set of rubric criteria. This proposal is then passed to Expert 2 for review. Expert 2 provides feedback and iterates with Expert 1 until the pair is approved. Finally, Expert 3 conducts a final, independent review and makes any last adjustments.
mismatch_note: 它给出了一套可复制的“专家写准则”流程（起草-审阅-终审），但同样没有报告 rubric 内容的标注者一致性——三专家是分工/审校关系，不是独立双写后比对，因此无法量化“若换一组专家，准则集合会差多少”。人机一致性指标仍是判分一致（macro-F1），不是覆盖率。准则数量梯度（20–43 条/prompt）对我们比对“单 rubric 覆盖多少条”是有用的规模参照。

their_construct: ClinConsensus：2,500 个中文医学开放病例，每例固定 30 条专家定义的二值准则（全库 75,000 条准则实例，约 42% 只属于单个病例），由 141 名执业医师按两条轴（common vs case-specific、broad vs granular）撰写，每例由非作者的医生复核，资深医师再随机审计 ~20%。评测指标 CACS@k（Clinician-Anchored Coverage Score）在 k=10 处把“回答命中了多少条医生准则”做成阈值化覆盖分，阈值由 135 名医生写的参考回答的经验均值标定。一致性方面比较两个独立医生组的 rubric 判定，用 Macro-F1。
their_finding: 11 个前沿模型上，两独立医生组的 pooled MF1 为 0.706–0.837（均值 0.772）；病例级 MF1 低值尾部集中在“边界回答”。模型侧 Rubric Accuracy 39.6%–52.1%，而 CACS@10 只有 17.8%–32.9%，形成 19.2–21.9 个百分点的覆盖缺口——作者据此主张应测“阈值化覆盖”而非平均部分正确率。
evidence_quote: Table 3 and Figure 3 show substantial but non-uniform physician agreement. Across the 11 models, pooled MF1 ranges from 0.706 to 0.837 (mean 0.772), highest for DeepSeek V3.2, GPT-5.2, and Grok 4.1 Fast, and lowest for Kimi K2.5 and Claude Opus 4.6.
mismatch_note: 它的“coverage”是**回答覆盖医生准则的比例**，不是**生成 rubric 覆盖专家准则的比例**——同名不同构念，必须分清。可复用的是：(i) 固定准则条数（每例 30 条）使跨例覆盖度可比，这直接对应我们“覆盖率的可枚举分母”；(ii) 用两套独立医生组估计“应用准则”的可靠性（0.706–0.837），这是我们做 golden-rub 噪声上界时可以借的范式。不可复用的是：它仍然把准则集当给定真值，未测准则写作一致性，且领域限于中文临床、准则由参考回答锚定。

their_construct: LEGIT：24K 量级法律推理数据；把法院判决转成“双方论点 + 法院结论”的层级 legal issue tree，再把每个 issue 转成 rubric——LLM judge 对每条 issue 同时判 coverage（回答是否提到该 issue）与 correctness（结论是否正确）。真值来自法院判决本身（不是另请专家从零写准则）；test split 300 例由作者人工检查修正。可靠性用两名持照韩国律师对随机 44 题的 issue 判定，对律师-律师、律师-LLM 算 Krippendorff's α。
their_finding: 两名律师在 LEGIT rubric 上的 Krippendorff's α = 0.87（阈值 0.67），作者据此称准则客观无歧义；强 LLM（GPT-4.1、Gemini-2.5-Pro）与律师达到显著一致，弱开源模型一致率低。与粗粒度 Likert 评分相比，LEGIT 的模块化 rubric 显著提高 LLM-judge 一致性。
evidence_quote: Lawyers achieve Krippendorff’s α score of 0.87, where the typically recommended threshold is α >0.67 (Krippendorff, 2006; Stefanovitch and Piskorski, 2023).
mismatch_note: 这是我们最接近“准则级、可枚举、有专家验证”的 golden-rub 形态之一，且提供了一条可复用的强证据链：issue tree 的节点数就是覆盖率的天然分母，α=0.87 说明“判某 issue 是否被覆盖”这件事人类可高一致完成。但关键差别是：真值准则不是专家独立撰写的产物，而是由 LLM 从判决书中抽取、再人工修正/抽检（构造流程见 §3.4），因此它测的是“从既有判决结构抽取准则”的可靠性，而不是“专家从任务出发枚举准则”的可靠性；α 也是在“应用准则”层面测的，不是准则集合本身的一致性。

their_construct: PLAWBENCH：850 道真实法律实务题（公共法律咨询 / 实务案例分析 / 法律文书生成），约 12,500 条 expert-designed rubric item，三任务平均 9.83 / 14.1 / 25 条/题。39 名法律专家（均通过国家统一法律职业资格考试）参与，选出 17 名资深标注者主导交叉验证；每例平均 3 小时、成本 >100 RMB；rubric 采用“结论 → 案情 → 分析 → 法律依据”四段式并配固定扣分规则；另用 3 名人类法律专家对抽样回答打分，与人选出的 LLM judge 做 Pearson/Spearman 对齐。
their_finding: 作者明确表示法律推理不存在唯一正确答案、不同学说框架均可成立，因此“Cohen's kappa 之类常规 inter-annotator agreement 指标不完全适用于本设定”，改用“分析过程是否合法理”的资深审校与 20% 案例二次外审；LLM judge 与人类专家分数的相关性被用来挑选 judge（Gemini-3.0-Pro-Preview）。
evidence_quote: Therefore, conventional inter-annotator agreement measures such as Cohen’s kappa are not fully appropriate for this setting.
mismatch_note: 这是本子域最重要的**反面样板**：它拥有 12,500 条准则级专家 rubric，却在协议层面放弃了一致性数值，只用“审校 + 抽样外审 + 下游评分相关性”替代。对我们意味着：(i) 高价值领域（法律/医学）的专家准则集，其“可复现性”可能本质上不可用 kappa 表达，我们若主张 golden-rub 是真值，就必须自己定义并报告一种“准则集一致性”的度量（如独立双写后的集合重合/匹配率），而不能引用现成 IAA；(ii) 它的一致性是在“回答打分”层面（Pearson/Spearman）而非“准则集合”层面。

their_construct: Interventional Transfer：在 HealthBench 分层抽样的 105 题上，把“如何评估生成的 rubric”重构成干预实验——对回答做最小编辑，使其通过/不通过目标 rubric（生成 rubric 或专家 rubric），再看另一套 rubric 上准则状态的净变化 Q。对比四类既有指标：(a) RubricRAG 式 LLM 语义匹配（0–9 分，取 max 得 recall/precision/F1）；(b) GenRubric 式分数相关（8 个响应模型的 Spearman）；(c) 医生回答上的分数相关；(d) 区分医生回答 vs 故意劣化回答。生成器为 Qwen3.8-27B、Deepseek-V4-Flash、Opus-5，响应模型 GPT-5.6-Terra，判分 Gemini 3.8 Flash 三票多数。
their_finding: 既有指标全部落在 0.3–0.75 的“中等”区间且生成器之间几乎无显著差异；但同一实现细节即可让 LLM-matching 的 F1 从约 0.5 掉到 0.1。准则级干预显示：最初未通过的生成准则中 82–87% 对专家 rubric 完全“不相关”（干预它不移动任何专家准则），而最初通过的只有 47–57%；专家 rubric 自身冗余度最高（通过项 53%、未通过项 29% 存在冗余）。此外，让回答“通过生成 rubric”只在 Opus-5 上带来 11% 的专家准则增益，说明生成 rubric 作为优化目标有系统性缺口。
evidence_quote: In the first three rows, interventions on generated criteria measured by expert rubrics, we observe a higher rate of irrelevance in initially failing criteria of $82-87$\% compared to $47-57$\% for initially passing.
mismatch_note: 这是本轮最强的**方法学锚点+间接证据**，但构念仍是“回答行为上的迁移”而非“准则集合的静态覆盖”：它能说“这些生成准则与专家准则行为上不相干”，却无法枚举“漏掉了哪几条专家准则”，也无法给出 per-instance 覆盖率。规模小（105 题、3 个生成器）。它对我们最有价值的两点：(i) 提供了对 coverage 类指标的效度警告——语义匹配分数对口径极敏感，我们的覆盖率必须配匹配器 IAA；(ii) 提示“专家 rubric 自身冗余”（53% 通过项冗余）会压低“多 rubric 并集”的边际收益，这与我们 P3 的“存在上限”预测直接相关，必须作为备择解释排除。

their_construct: 在 HealthBench meta-evaluation 数据（29,511 个 prompt×completion×rubric，60,896 条医生标注，186 名医生，34 条 consensus criteria）上做方差分解：label ~ 1 + (1|physician) + (1|rubric) 的线性混合模型，再对 case-level disagreement 做以 rubric 为唯一随机效应的分解；并用 metadata、rubric 语言、专科、表面特征、embedding、共识校验的 uncertainty 类别解释残差。
their_finding: 整体医生分歧率 22.5%。rubric identity 解释 15.8% 的 met/not-met 标签方差，但只解释 3.6–6.9% 的分歧方差；医生 identity 只解释 2.4%；81.8% 是 case-level 残差，且不能被元数据、rubric 措辞、专科、表面特征或 embedding 降低。分歧随完成质量呈倒 U（清楚好/清楚坏时一致，边界病例才分裂）；可约不确定性（缺上下文、措辞模糊）把分歧 odds 提高 2.55 倍，但只解释约 3% 总方差。作者据此认为 HealthBench GPT-4.1 的 MF1=0.709 被 22.5% 的人类分歧机械性封顶。
evidence_quote: Rubric identity accounts for 15.8% of met/not-met label variance but only 3.6–6.9% of disagreement variance; physician identity accounts for just 2.4%.
mismatch_note: 它直接处理我们 D5 的核心风险：golden-rub 不是无噪声真值。但它测的是“同一套既定准则下医生判分是否一致”，不是“专家会不会写出不同的准则集”。对我们的推论是双面的：(i) 正面——分歧主要来自 case 本身而非准则，说明只要准则集固定，判分可靠性可接受；(ii) 反面——如果 81.8% 的残差是 case-level pattern noise，那么“覆盖率”这类把准则集当作客观分母的指标，其上限就受限于“哪些准则算适用于该例”这一判断本身的不可约分歧，我们必须在协议里显式处理（例如报告准则适用性的多标注者一致性，而不只报覆盖数值）。

their_construct: Judge-free 'authoring vs execution' asymmetry on four reference constructions: (a) COMPLETE TRUTH = a mechanically decidable predicate ('contains a double letter', '>=8 letters', 'contains th', 'ends in s') over a presented 15-word list (n=240), plus a numeric-predicate variant over presented integer lists; (b) EXECUTABLE TRUTH = HumanEval+/MBPP+ tests authored from the docstring and scored by a hardened oracle solution pool (1,560 oracle-correct / 904 oracle-wrong); (c) LEXICAL TRUTH = WordNet synsets (n=240). Authoring = emit the acceptable set S-hat (extensional) or a suite whose induced acceptance region is S-hat (intensional); execution = pointwise membership judgment on one presented candidate. Both arms scored as binary classifiers over the same candidates (set F1, recall, precision). Models: Qwen2.5 3B-72B, Qwen3-14B/32B, Llama-3.2-3B/3.1-8B, Mistral-7B, Phi-4, gemma-4-12B, GPT-5.1, Claude Opus 4.8. Omission audit: a drafted key is corrupted with planted over-inclusions or planted omissions; detection rate is corrected by the reviewer's false-alarm rate on a clean key (signal-detection statistic d = D - F).
their_finding: Authoring/enumeration sits below judging in every model x construction cell and does not catch up over a 24x scale range: complete truth authoring F1 0.259->0.483 vs judging 0.599->0.769 (gaps +0.34/+0.25/+0.29/+0.29, disjoint CIs); on code, judging F1 0.74-0.90 while authored suites admit only 19-42% of oracle-correct solutions (and 94-99.8% of wrong ones are still caught). The same models write an executable predicate for the identical sets at F1 0.978-0.999 (100% executable), so the deficit is materialization/enumeration, not knowledge or specification ability. Omission is the dominant and audit-resistant error: planted over-inclusions are detected 6-7x more often than planted omissions (7B 0.706 vs 0.100 = 7.1x; 14B 0.860 vs 0.148 = 5.8x; 72B 0.860 vs 0.375 = 2.3x, and 72B narrows only by flooding the key with unsupported additions, false alarms 1.1->5.46/item). A production K-12 corpus (43,227 scored items, ten generator LLMs) shows evaluator-diagnosed answer-key errors split 316 omissions : 33 over-inclusions (~10:1), 'consistent across all ten generators' (observational, judge-relative, authors flag it as the weakest link). Subtractive/self review therefore removes visible over-inclusions while retaining invisible omissions, shifting artifacts toward under-acceptance. Same-model sample-then-verify repair is falsified: K=10 union recall <=0.55, and even K=16 sampling reaches union recall only 0.707/0.797/0.842 at 7B/14B/72B against execution recall ~0.95-0.98; the missing members 'are not hiding in the sampling distribution'.
evidence_quote: The dominant error is \emph{omission}, and omission resists audit: an over-inclusion is a written token a reviewer can challenge, while a missing member is an absence whose discovery is the authoring problem itself. Models detect planted over-inclusions $6$--$7\times$ more often than planted omissions, and a production deployment of $43{,}227$ scored items fails omission-first at $10{:}1$.
mismatch_note: Construct differs at the level that matters for our novelty claim. Their S* is a set of acceptable MEMBERS satisfying a membership predicate over a candidate universe (word list / synset / code-solution pool), scored by set-F1/recall; it is NOT a set of rubric CRITERIA, and rubric criteria have no membership oracle over a candidate space. 'Enumerated rubrics' appear only as an asserted analogue ('extensionally for answer keys and enumerated rubrics', L753; also L257) and are never operationalized or measured. On the four verification questions: (1) NO cross-model missed-set comparison. Each model authors the same items but only per-model recall/set-F1 is reported; there is no Jaccard or co-occurrence matrix of omitted members across models/families (zero occurrences of 'jaccard'; 'multi-model' appears only as untested: 'tool-augmented or multi-model authoring pipelines remain untested', L1296). (2) NO statistical test separating systematic from idiosyncratic omission. 'Systematically under-accepting' (L957) is a directional claim; the support for cross-sample stability is that same-model resampling does not recover the omissions ('the missing members of SSsilent are not hiding in the sampling distribution', L1031) plus K=16 union-recall saturation (Table L2129-2136, recall 0.707/0.797/0.842 vs execution ceiling ~0.95-0.98). Cross-generator evidence is only the direction of the field-corpus taxonomy ('consistent across all ten generators', L1192), not an overlap statistic. (3) Per-item omission rates are NOT reported; only a per-PREDICATE authoring-F1 table (L1944-1949: '>=8 letters' 0.61-0.76 easiest, 'ends in s' 0.19-0.32 hardest), so 'which side is missed' is answered at predicate-type granularity only. (4) The mechanism (autoregressive emission with no lookahead and a learned stopping rule, L308-313) is tied to unordered finite sets of 4-30 members; rubric criteria sets are short, semantically driven, and have no decidable boundary, so neither the mechanism nor the effect sizes are guaranteed to transfer. Likewise their code arm FAILS in the opposite direction (over-specification/invented requirements), showing the omission story is construction-specific. This is mechanism-level support for 'LLM-authored specification sets systematically under-cover and the gap is hard to audit', not a measurement of rubric criteria coverage or cross-rubric complementarity.

their_construct: Intrinsic rubric-quality measurement: import measurement theory (Lawshe CVR from a 5-persona GPT-5.5 panel; 5-level domain map; cross-lens objective relevance; weight calibration) into a 17-signal vector, plus the RIFT taxonomy of 9 failure modes under reliability and content validity. 'Missing Criteria' is one of the nine (Content Validity -> Under-Specification). Validation is causal injection: 8 criterion-level operators on 60 expert rubrics (GDPval 30 + Terminal-Bench 30) at rho=0.5 (480 variants) plus rho=0.25/0.75 on a 15-task subset (240), 9th mode weight-level; signals recover the injected mode at 75.0% vs 56.7% for claude-opus-4-8. Reference instrument is an LLM-generated persona panel/domain map, not an independent expert gold rubric.
their_finding: Missing Criteria is an explicitly named, content-validity failure mode: 'a prompt requirement that no criterion evaluates' (appendix/rift.tex:81,272). It is operationalized only as a deterministic corruption that deletes a sampled rho fraction of criteria (appendix/rift.tex:498-500), and its signature is purely structural: item counts fall (d=-2.30; dose slope on total_items -13.3, labeled 'Mechanical', appendix/experiments_overflow.tex:91,164) and representativeness falls d=-0.38 ('Surviving criteria stay individually healthy; only composition shifts', appendix/experiments_overflow.tex:95), while per-criterion content validity is unaffected (sections/experiments.tex:49).
evidence_quote: Apply when the prompt implies at least one checkable must-have requirement, but the rubric provides no criterion that allows a grader to evaluate that requirement at all.
mismatch_note: Different construct at the load-bearing joint. (1) Their 'coverage' is a rubric set vs an LLM-generated objective blueprint/domain map: representativeness = 1 - JSD(W||A) with realized coverage A_j proportional to sum_i s_i R_ij, explicitly 'measures construct underrepresentation' (sections/quality_signals.tex:62; sections/quality_signals.tex:32: 'whether the set covers the domain in the right proportions'). They never compute rubric-A criterion set vs rubric-B (golden/expert) criterion set, so their primitive does not directly transfer to 'single-rub coverage of golden-rub' without substituting the blueprint for a human gold rubric. (2) Missing criteria is never observed in naturally occurring or LLM-generated rubrics; it is injected by deleting sampled criteria, so the paper says nothing about which criteria models systematically omit, or whether omissions overlap across generators/models (the L1 systematicity question). Authors concede this: 'These interventions do not fully capture naturally occurring rubric defects' (sections/limitations.tex:12). (3) Their notion is prompt-requirement-relative, ours is golden-criterion-relative; a requirement may be omitted, or a gold criterion may be absent from the prompt. Net: supports the premise that omission is a real, distinct, measurable failure mode and supplies a name plus a quantitative coverage primitive, but neither threatens P1's novelty (no single-rub-vs-golden measurement) nor supplies evidence on H1(a)-systematicity.

their_construct: Audit of expert-authored rubrics themselves as measurement instruments: score the 60 human-authored rubrics (48 with a non-constant CVR vector) with weight-calibration statistics against the N=5 LLM persona panel, specifically ordering calibration rho_ord = Spearman(|w_i|, CVR_i) and core weight share.
their_finding: Expert-authored gold rubrics are not defect-free: on 48 scoreable rubrics mean rho_ord = +0.195 but 10 of 48 are negative (anti-calibrated), putting more scoring mass on criteria the expert panel judged less essential, so a response can fail the core requirement and still score well. The other 12 rubrics have constant CVR and are left unscored. Missing-criteria prevalence in these same 60 expert rubrics is NOT reported.
evidence_quote: There still remains a substantial minority: 10 of 48 scoreable rubrics are negative, ranking criteria against panel-rated necessity, so the rubric awards more credit for the less essential criterion of a pair.
mismatch_note: Ground-truth caveat, not evidence for/against P1 under the same construct. It shows an expert golden-rub can be invalid on the WEIGHT axis, so a golden-rub must be audited rather than assumed valid; but it measures weighting (rho_ord vs an LLM panel), not criterion-set completeness/coverage, and it uses an LLM-generated panel (GPT-5.5 with shared blind spots, sections/limitations.tex:22) instead of a human gold standard. It therefore raises a validity caveat for our groundtruth target without supplying any number on how incomplete expert rubrics are, and it does not measure omission/systematicity at all.

their_construct: Mutation-testing analogy for rubrics: a rubric is a test suite, a response the program under test. Stage 1 mines reusable mutation operators from 1,000 OpenRubrics preferred/dispreferred pairs; Stage 2 generates an initial rubric + reference response, injects verified defects, and calls a defect 'sufficiently detected' if the rubric's score drops by delta_total=8 (0-100 aggregate) OR by delta_item=2 (0-4 item scale); under-penalized defects are fed to an LLM refiner and the refinement is kept only if retesting improves penalization. Evaluated on 703 tasks (574 RubricBench STEM/Code/IF/Chat + 129 RM-Bench Chat) across 4 domains against 6 baselines (TICK, RLCF-C/R/B, Dynamic, MRRG); backbones GPT-5.4-mini and Gemini-2.5-flash-lite each used as BOTH rubric generator and judge; auxiliary LLM fixed to GPT-5.4. Reported metric is pairwise preference accuracy only.
their_finding: Mubric reaches 57.27% overall accuracy vs the strongest baseline MRRG at 49.78% (+7.48 points), highest in 8/10 dataset-LLM settings and significant in 7. Ablation (Gemini-2.5-flash-lite): Initial 47.94, Direct-Refine 45.38, On-the-Fly Ops 44.24, full Mubric 51.78. The paper never reports a coverage/recall number against any expert rubric, never applies the mutation probe to the 6 baselines, and never measures overlap or union across generators.
evidence_quote: If an injected defect causes little or no score reduction, \ours interprets this as evidence that the corresponding quality requirement is insufficiently captured by the rubric and refines the rubric accordingly.
mismatch_note: NOT our construct, and not the 'orthogonal-to-downstream-scoring coverage measure' the screening rationale hoped for. The mutation probe is an internal REFINEMENT signal; the reported result is downstream pairwise accuracy (sections/Experiments.tex:L25). Verifying the 4 full-text questions: (1) NO per-method report of under-penalized defect types — the probe is never run on TICK/RLCF/Dynamic/MRRG, so 'do different generators miss the same requirement class' (L1 core) is untested; (2) NO criterion-level coverage metric against a golden rubric — item-level score drops exist (sections/Method.tex:L65-70) but are only thresholded per-mutation, never aggregated into recall/coverage; (3) operators are mined from preference pairs and skewed (see record 2609.37322#b); (4) coverage judgment is NOT independent of the generator — the same LLM judge J generates the initial rubric and scores the mutations, and the ground truth for the final metric is preference labels (RubricBench/RM-Bench), not an expert criterion set. It supports H1(a) only indirectly: the Initial-vs-Mubric gap (47.94 -> 51.78) shows a single generated rubric leaves some injected requirement types unpenalized, but gives no coverage magnitude, no per-instance distribution, and no cross-generator structure.

their_construct: Stage-1 mutation-operator construction and RQ3 analysis: from 1,000 OpenRubrics tasks (task description + preferred/dispreferred pair), an LLM extracts concrete response defects, then abstracts them along two axes — transformation type and affected quality aspect (the 12 FLASK dimensions) — into operators o=(t,a,c,iota). RQ3 reports the operator inventory (Figure 2) and the top-3 quality aspects / transformation types selected per evaluation dataset.
their_finding: 201 reusable operators. Transformation types: Omit 34, Distort Form 29, Break Logic 27, Misalign Intent 25, Fabricate 24. Quality aspects are concentrated on Logical Correctness 43, Factuality 31, Comprehension 22, Logical Robustness 21; i.e. the mined defect universe is not spread over the 12 FLASK dimensions but dominated by four substantive-correctness ones. Selection is domain-conditioned: Code picks Logical Correctness 70% / Break Logic 31%; STEM picks Factuality 43% / Fabricate 34%; IF picks Comprehension 48% / Distort Form 28% / Omit 26%.
evidence_quote: Across quality aspects, they are concentrated primarily on Logical Correctness (43), Factuality (31), Comprehension (22), and Logical Robustness (21)
mismatch_note: A methodological caution, not H-evidence. The probe set is not neutral: operators are mined from preferred/dispreferred pairs and binned onto FLASK's 12 dimensions, and 4 of the 12 absorb most mass. A mutation-based coverage probe can therefore only expose omissions along the mined aspects — an apparently complete rubric may simply be untested on the un-mined aspects, which would mimic 'low omission' for the wrong reason. This directly warns against adopting defect-mining from preference pairs as a neutral ground truth for our coverage denominator. Also: 'common defects' are biased by the response distribution in OpenRubrics (and the paper confirms zero task overlap with the 703 eval tasks, so it is at least not leakage).

their_construct: All-must-pass checklist rubric (k atomic checks; an output passes iff every check answers Yes). Each labeled output is treated as a cooperative game over checks: F_i = the set of checks answered No, v_i(S)=1[S∩F_i≠∅]. Proposition: the Shapley value of check j is exactly 1/|F_i| if j∈F_i and 0 otherwise. Summing over labeled outputs gives each check a catch credit C_j (summed on flawed outputs) and a false-fail blame B_j (summed on correct outputs); a check holds a 'unique catch' on output i iff F_i={j}. Exact and O(nk), no sampling. Applied on synthetic Recon (12 cloud-security environments), plus SummEdits and RAGTruth; judges Claude Sonnet/Haiku/Opus.
their_finding: Under all-must-pass aggregation every check gets an exact closed-form Shapley attribution — catch credit, false-fail blame, and a count of unique catches — computable in one linear pass over the judge's per-check answers. Unique catches operationalize which check does work no other check does; credit that is shared among checks does not protect a check from deletion.
evidence_quote: A check holds a \emph{unique catch} on flawed output $i$ when $F_i = \{j\}$: removing it would let that output pass. By efficiency, credits sum to the number of flawed outputs caught and blames to the number of correct outputs failed, so the two headline rates decompose exactly over checks.
mismatch_note: Unique-catch/credit/blame is computed over one rubric's checks relative to labeled outputs (which single check is the only one failing a given output), i.e. WITHIN-rubric redundancy at the output-verdict level. It is NOT cross-rubric overlap between two single-LLM criterion sets, nor coverage of a golden/expert criterion set. It therefore offers a reusable per-criterion redundancy/complementarity statistic (the criterion-level analogue of our H1(b) overlap measure) and a methodological anchor, but does not itself test P1/H1 as we define them. Also specific to all-must-pass aggregation; other aggregators change the game.

their_construct: Self-review drift experiment: start from a hand-written rubric (H) and a label-taught rubric (L, produced by revising the generated draft against 36 labeled calibration reports) on Recon; a reviser revises all 12 environments for 4 rounds under a generic 'review for ambiguity, gaps, misreadings, uncaught flaws' instruction. Arms: Opus (2 seeds), Sonnet, Haiku; Opus with check count fixed; Opus delete/merge-only. Replicated on SummEdits and RAGTruth. Metrics: correct outputs passed, flawed outputs caught, and 'unplanned caught' — a real exposure outside the planted scenario that rubric authors and revisers never saw.
their_finding: Starting from the label-taught rubric, every free/fixed-count reviser disables the same open completeness/coverage check in a different way: Opus deletes it as 'the vague completeness check', Sonnet rewrites it into a closed list of expected items, Haiku writes the answer into it. Catch of unanticipated omissions collapses (100% -> 25.0%/8.3% for Opus, 25.0% Sonnet, 66.7% Haiku; fixed-count 16.7%). Only delete-only revision left the metrics at starting values. In every L arm the lost catches were all unplanned misses; the 60 planted-flaw catches were untouched.
evidence_quote: Three revisers, three ways of closing the same check (Appendix~\ref{app:recon}). In every L arm the lost catches were all unplanned misses; the 60 planted-flaw catches were untouched.
mismatch_note: Omission here is induced by model self-REVIEW of an existing rubric, not by one-shot single-LLM generation compared against a golden criterion set; 'unplanned caught' is measured against a task ground-truth exposure, not a golden rubric criterion set. All three revisers are Claude (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku), so the cross-model systematicity is demonstrated only within one family (authors themselves flag the drift direction may be family-specific). Still, it is direct evidence that omission of coverage criteria is directed and reproducible across models, not random — relevant to the 'systematic omission' (L1) premise.

their_construct: Per-check Shapley attribution of the 186 checks deleted across the 12 Recon revision chains: for each deleted check, did it hold a unique catch (the only check failing some flawed output) and did it carry any false-fail blame, broken down by check origin (tracked across revisions by text similarity to the parent check).
their_finding: Of 186 deleted checks, 179 had caught at least one flawed report and 78 (about 42%) held a unique catch — including 56 of the 71 deleted label-derived checks — while only 2 (about 1%) carried any false-fail blame. Self-review thus removes exactly the checks that do work no other check does and keeps/adds the checks that fail correct outputs, the opposite of what an improving revision would do. The unique-vs-blame asymmetry is a quantitative, directional signature of systematic omission rather than noise.
evidence_quote: of 186 deleted checks, 179 had caught at least one flawed report and 78 held a unique catch, among them 56 of the 71 deleted label-derived checks. Only 2 of the 186 carried any false-fail blame.
mismatch_note: Measures the deletion behavior of a revision process, not the coverage content of an initial single-LLM rubric against a golden criterion set; 'unique catch' is within-rubric and output-level, not criterion-set-level. Uses Claude revisers only.
